analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Justice Bremen, we will hear arguments first this morning in number 349, United States Against Holstowski and the Consolidated Case. Mr. Stavis, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, I may it please for court. There are two cases here. Number 536, our petition. Number 349, the Solicited General's petition. The facts in both cases are quite simple. Part 46, which I will deal with first, involves the jurisdiction of the District Court to try this indictment. And the facts there are, obviously, the indictment itself, which charges a member of Congress with taking money and conspiring to take money for introducing bills in Congress, bills which the indictment charges will in fact introduce, and the bills are specifically identified in the indictment. It is plain from the face of the indictment that the grand jury which found it, heard, considered, and relied upon proof of the performance of legislative acts. And while it is not clear from the indictment, it is established in the opinion of Judge Mina and undisputed, that the indicting grand jury, as the grand jury which handed down this indictment, received proof of the performance of legislative acts from the United States Attorney, not from Mr. Hostosky. It is also clear and undisputed that while Mr. Hostosky gave legislative materials to earlier grand juries, not the indicting grand jury, he had no reason to believe at the time that he gave such materials, that he was the target of the grand jury. And in fact, somebody else was thereafter indicted, tried, and convicted. Of course, it wouldn't make any difference to your theory if he had, would it? If he was a target... If he was aware that he was... I knew he was. To our fundamental theory, it doesn't... Might have something to do with the waiver. I don't think it has anything to do with waiver either, but I agree that if our theory is correct, that this is a jurisdictional allocation, then it wouldn't make any difference at all. Who was the other person under inquiry? Another member of Congress? No, no. Somebody who had been employed by the Congressman some eight years previously. Was not then employed, and hadn't been employed for many, many years. Now, our position in 546 is, and you put your finger right on it, that the court had no jurisdiction to try this indictment. And if the court agrees with us on that, of course, it doesn't have to reach the evidentiary issues which were involved in 349. Now, I'm not going to attempt to match the eloquence of this court and its eight opinions dealing with the speech and debate clause and review or recount the history of that clause and its meaning in England and in the United States. Mr. Davis, are you going to get it all to the appealability of Judge Meiner's order by the government? I noticed that you attacked it in the Third Circuit, but neither party apparently contests it here. It would seem to me that it is not open and shut that that was an appealable order. Well, in the Third Circuit, we certainly didn't believe that it was an appealable order. We moved to dismiss before the Third Circuit on those grounds. The Third Circuit denied our motion. I must confess that we did not cause petition on that particular issue, but it may very well be appropriate for the court to address that question on its own motion. We have jurisdiction of the Court of Appeals opinion judgment only if it was properly in the Court of Appeals. I don't think this matter was properly in the Court of Appeals. Candidly, I don't think the issue which the government presented in its petition or even properly before this Court because the entire factual foundation for the government's petition in 349 is a series of proposed proffers of proof which they asked the District Court to rule upon three times, and the District Court refused to do so. So there are no facts before this Court, and 349 is a wholly and an entirely supposititious case. And in that respect, I guess I don't have to call your attention, the attention of the Court, the dissenting opinion by Ms. Justice Blackmun concurred in by the Chief Justice only last week in the Portage case, which you addressed the question of the proposition that this Court oughtn't to be handling supposititious cases. It's got enough business handling concrete issues. And while the other seven members of the Court didn't agree that that principle applied to that case, there's no question that this Court ordinarily tries and adjudicates only concrete cases. Well, that I guess that's a case in controversy argument, but that I understand, Mr. Stavis, you're suggesting that even though you did not cross-petition on the question of the appealability of the order of the Third Circuit, that it's jurisdictional and therefore that we can reach and decide it. I accepted the suggestion of Mr. Justice Rehnquist. I just want to be clear. Now, the argument you're now making is really a case of controversy argument. That's correct. And that's a separate argument, is it? That's correct. All right. May I get back to the issues in 546, which is the jurisdiction of this Court to try, of the district Court, of an Article III Court, to try this indictment? That the speech and debate clause establishes jurisdictional allocation comes all through the decisions of this Court, including its latest. And that, of course, is the Chief Justice's opinion in Eastland against Servicemen's Union. For the Court. I'm sorry? Opinion for the Court. Of course. The opinion for the Court. And what you addressed there was the fact that the speech and debate clause affects the availability of judicial power. Now, the corollary to approaching this matter from the point of view of jurisdiction or the availability of judicial power is that no one says that members of Congress are super citizens, and the speech and debate clause gives them free license to take bribes and commit crimes and introduce bills that are paid for. That the only question is, which is the proper courthouse? Is it an Article III Court or is it the Congress of the United States under both the speech and debate clause and the punishment clause? And so there's no question about it. My client never has, does not now, nor will he, contest the jurisdiction of the Congress of the United States to try the charges which are involved with here. He's not exactly looking to be charged. Can they try these charges now? I believe so. And what was the sanction that Congress imposed? If I read Kilburn against Thompson, the Congress has complete power to impose any sanctions it chooses, including, if I read Kilburn against Thompson correctly, imprisonment. That's what you say in Kilburn. I suppose under the Constitution it wouldn't be authorized to impose a cruel or unusual punishment. Oh, I think there are constitutional limitations upon the exercise of its power. That's power against McCormick. We expect that if we are tried on this by Congress, we expect to insist upon a due process hearing. And a whole panoply of rights that would be applied to any judicial hearing, and that would be a judicial hearing. It's just an exception to Article III jurisdiction. You're going to insist on a jury trial? No. No, we don't expect it to be a jury trial. Although the Constitution guarantees that, doesn't it? It guarantees it in an Article III trial. I do not believe that it would be... It's something about an Article III trial, does it? Well, I would guess, however, that we would accept the fact that it would not be a jury trial. If we were entitled to a jury trial, we would wait it. I think the essence of the punishment clause is that the Congress itself has that power. Subject to what constitutional limitations? Subject to due process limitations. But not a jury trial. That's correct. Subject to cruel and unusual punishment limitations. Presumption of innocence. Presumption of innocence. Necessity of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. I believe so. Right of confrontation. Right of cross-examination. Right of counsel. Mr. Davis, is it clear that that clause applies to a former Congressman? Congress in the past has so asserted, we do not dispute that. And besides, as of the time that this indictment was found, Mr. Hustoski was a member of Congress. Yes, but he's not now. Any punishment by Congress would be from now on. That is correct. And we do not dispute the jurisdiction of Congress, but the point that I'm making is... You don't here because you don't have to. That is correct. And all we have to dispute here is the jurisdiction of the Article III court. The courts don't have any jurisdiction. And at the time that this indictment was found, Congress clearly had jurisdiction. But what would be... Is there a stage of limitations in this? I don't know that there is any. Well, Mr. Davis, what you said Congress has asserted authority to try after his defeat, which I gather is what happened to this Congress. That's correct. Has that ever happened? Yes, it has. Against whom? Well, Mr. Brown, speaking for the Speaker, will address that particular question. Historically, it has occurred. I think, in fact, it occurred in the most famous corruption investigation by the Congress in the Credit Mobilier transaction, where Congressman Oaks Ames was charged, tried, and convicted by the House after he was no longer sitting. And I think there are a number of other examples of that sort. Mr. Davis, would the net result of accepting your theory mean that Congress could not enact and the President sign a law making it a criminal offense for a congressman to take a bribe? Congress has enacted such a law, and such a law is on the books and has been enforced and is valid, but not in respect to the performance of legislative acts. In other words, the Johnson case, which wasn't, in fact, tried under that section, is a perfect example. A congressman takes a bribe to try to influence the Department of Justice. the normal conflict of interest situation or to take a bribe for an act which is not a legislative act in nature. What the speech and debate clause is driving that is that if you want to try a legislative act, fraud in connection with the legislative act, if you want to try the legislative process, that belongs in the Congress. if you want to try just the question of bribery, not implicating the legislative process, that you may do in an article-free court. But when, Mr. Stavis, when the charge is for taking money in exchange for a promise of a future act, hasn't the court held that it's not necessary to show the legislative act or the legislative activity? And of course, that's your opinion in the Brewster case. That's exactly what the court held. And the whole point of the government taking this case is that they want to get around that decision. Because in that decision, you said at least eight times, we counted them, that under the Brewster indictment, you could not show the actual performance of a legislative act. Well, how will we know whether the government is going to try to prove that until the case is tried? Well, that's what we thought, accepting that the government, and that's why we don't think you would even consider this case, but the government says, please look at our profits of proof. This is really what we want to prove. We say, those people aren't even going to testify that way, let alone the fact that if they did testify, it wouldn't be true. But the government is asking you to make, asking the district court, and asking you to make rulings on advanced evidentiary proof. I understand you say you didn't want us to hear this case? We want you to hear the government's petition. Oh, I see. We want you to hear the government's petition. I see. I see. Sure, I want you to hear my petition. I see. Because my petition. I just marvel at your fairness. Well, I think it's not only fair but correct. But let me get back, Mr. Chief Justice, to your question, because you said that in Brewster, and you looked at an indictment that did not charge the performance of legislative acts. Look at this indictment. on its face, it charges the specific performance of designated and named legislative acts. Now, if this case goes to trial, and if you prove, if the government is permitted to prove the facts as alleged in this indictment, and they're talking about what would have happened if they came up with a booster indictment, but if they prove the facts alleged in this indictment, that jury is going to be asked to decide questions as to the functioning of the legislative process, specifically. What if the trial court excludes any evidence about the legislative acts? Well, that's what Judge Meena said he was going to do, and that's why the government took this case up. They weren't satisfied with Judge Meena's decision, which said, I read the Brewster opinion, and I intend to enforce it and not permit the introduction of legislative acts. The government took it up. That's why this case has been going on now for over two and a half years without a trial. Now, I want to emphasize that our position is that in the light of this indictment, the issue does not end with the fact that the government would not be permitted to introduce that evidence at trial. And that's what my petition is about. I say that the grand jury released and found an indictment which on its face is beyond the jurisdiction of this court. And what the government is saying is, well, let's fix up the indictment a little bit. Well, maybe they shouldn't have charged and alleged these legislative acts which they designate in that indictment. Well, just strike it out. Fix it up and make it like the Brewster type indictment and forget that it'll ever happen. Mr. Stavis, do you agree that if they strike the allegations of the specific overt act describing legislative acts, that the indictment would then be comparable to the indictment in the Brewster case? It's a little bit more than the specific legislative act. It's also the allegations in terms two, three, and four of the indictment, which also include allegations of specific legislative acts. Yes, the answer is, if all those words were taken out, then you have an indictment that led like the Brewster indictment. But the trouble about doing that is that by the issuance of the indictment, the executive branch of the government, the executive branch of the government, has implicated, executive branch of the grand jury, has implicated and impugned the functioning of Congress. Now, the point that we make is that when the speech or debate clause is set up to protect this delicate tripartite separation of powers, it means to protect... Well, Mr. Stavis, would you say then that if, before the defendant is put in jeopardy, the government had come in and voluntarily dismissed the indictment, got permission to dismiss the indictment, then re-indicted, leaving out all the references to legislative acts? No problem about that. They still would have done what you just said. No, provided that, now this is the difference, provided that it had not presented the legislative acts to the grand jury. Ah, so that having presented the legislative acts to the grand jury, they have given him permanent immunity? No, they haven't. There's nothing in the world that says that they can't call another grand jury and present a case to another grand jury. That's exactly what happened in the Lawn case. In the Lawn case, decided by this court. Your position, just so I get it, is that having told a particular grand jury about a legislative act by a congressman, that grand jury may never return an indictment against that congressman. Indictment which charges legislative acts. Well, I thought you said a moment ago if they dismissed the indictment and brought a new one that didn't make reference, it'd still be bad. Oh, no. No, what I mean is that they can't, I mean, obviously they can indict them for backwobling. Something having, they may be able to indict them for the backwobling. They just excise from the new indictment any reference to the legislative acts and they merely follow the pattern of the Brewster indictment. That would be invalid because the grand jury, the grand jury has violated the speech and debate clause, but this is not to say that the government cannot convene another grand jury, present a case which does not involve proof of legislative acts and come out with a Brewster type indictment. But that's like Calandra. Once the information has been presented to the grand jury, there's nothing more that can be done to salvage the speech and debate clause. The question is whether the indictment it returns is constitutional or not. The idea that if you presented different information to another grand jury, somehow you could call it back to, call the earlier proceedings back, just isn't possible. It is not like Calandra. Calandra is a very different kind of a case. In Calandra, you decided that under the Fourth Amendment, the exclusionary clause which is your making, that you would allow a grand jury to hear evidence unlawfully seized by somebody else. And we also said in Calandra that the right of privacy protected by the Fourth Amendment had already been breached it. And there was nothing that, no. I understand that. But here you have an explicit provision of the speech in the Constitution which says that speech or debate, which I wish we mean legislative acts, shall not be questioned in any other place and the value said that includes a grand jury. Did it say he may not be questioned or he may not be required to answer? It said he may not be questioned. I think it says may not be questioned. Now, did he have to respond to anything in the grand jury? I think he did at the point where he wasn't the target. As I read Gravel... Well, a lot of non-target witnesses before grand juries claim immunity from responding for various reasons. And the Fifth Amendment, yes. But there might be another reason here then, wouldn't there? Might be. But if I read the Gravel case accurately, and I think I do, there is no speech and debate protection and questioning when the grand jury is investigating third-party crime. Which states in my right that Bill Klein voluntarily gave the legislators stuff to the grand jury? He gave it to them voluntarily. So, is that... Do you take the position that if a congressman is up for anything and he voluntarily gives legislative things, he can't be indicted from then on? He's immunized forever? He wasn't up for anything. Yeah, but he voluntarily, didn't he? He did. He was subpoenaed to testify. But didn't he bring these bills there? He was subpoenaed to testify. And didn't he bring the bills there? That is correct. Didn't he bring the legislative matters there? That is correct. And now he complains about bringing them there. Because he believes... And now he complains about bringing them there. He doesn't complain about bringing them there. He thinks he was required to bring them there. He doesn't complain about that at all. What he complains about is some grand jury that he never brought them before and which turned the wheel and targeted him. He would be immunized and robbing a bank in the state of Alaska. Your Honor, I said exactly the contrary. I'm not too sure you wouldn't go so far as to say he'd be immunized from robbing the bank in Great Britain. Your Honor, I said exactly the contrary. I said that quite the contrary. He is subject to prosecution in an Article 3 court by a grand jury which doesn't have this material. He is subject to prosecution before Congress where this material may properly be the subject of inquiry by the court which has jurisdiction. So I do not accept the suggestion, Your Honor, because I think I've said exactly the contrary. May I reserve some of my time? Does it not sometimes happen, Mr. Savas, that the prosecution fails to prove all of what is alleged in indictment and yet a conviction nevertheless results? Of course that happens, but those are not cases where you're dealing with an expressed constitutional prescription. Now this trial judge has indicated that he will in advance have the advantage of his statement that he would not admit any testimony on that score. That he intends to comply with Brewster. But I just, our position is that the indictment is already a violation of the speech or debate clause. Therefore he can never be tried under this indictment. Under what indictment? Now, that what, these, this indictment has to be dismissed as your position. That's correct. And if he's to be indicted, he has to be indicted by a new grand jury, which does not hear the evidence that you say violates the speech. And that's not any different to what you give about. That is your position. That is correct. That's precisely the position. The statute of limitations. I'm sorry. What about the statute of limitations? I think there's an express provision of the statutes which provides that we're an indictment is voided for some reason, not having to do with the merits of the offense, that the statute of limitations is told. I think there's an express provision in the United States Code. where it is. No, but I'll be glad to furnish it to you. You have an idea. I can find it. It's in the United States Code. Good. But there's an express provision. I looked that up thinking about this case, and I did look it up. In fact, if you didn't remember it, it makes me think it might not help me. Well, it doesn't help me in the sense that a new indictment can be brought as I have suggested. In that sense, it doesn't help me. But it also makes clear that the suggestion I've made as to the potentialities of a new indictment is entirely feasible. And I just want to say, in reference to Mr. Justice Brennan's question, that of course is exactly what you do in an immunity case. You forbid the use of immunized testimony. You impose upon the prosecutor an obligation to establish that he didn't use immunized testimony when he got the indictment. If he can't make it, he can go to another grand jury. He can go to another grand jury and get an indictment without the use of the immunized testimony. He does that all the time. Is there any case from this court saying that an indictment returned that the government didn't show was not used based on immunized testimony is invalid? Well, I think Lorne comes close to that. Lorne, what you said was... Well, could you answer yes or no? I'm not sure I could put my fingers on a case at the moment. May I reserve some time? May I ask you, Mr. Davis? One question before you do. You mentioned the jurisdiction over former members would be covered in your colleague's argument, but as I look at his brief, he gives us an example of five former members over whom Congress did not have jurisdiction. Maybe he will cover it, but I would like to be advised on that if it's not right. I think he's given an example of cases in which former members of Congress were covered. You don't happen to know such a case yourself? Other than the Oaks-Ames case, which I mentioned. Mr. McClendon, could you give me that again? Oaks-Ames, Congressman Ames, Congressman Ames, involved in the credit mobile year controversy. It was around the 1870s, I think. That was the biggest scandal case in Congress at the time. Thank you very much. Mr. Brand. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, I am here representing the Honorable Thomas P. O'Neill Speaker, the Honorable Frank Thompson, Chairman, and the Honorable William Dickinson, Ranking Minority Member, Committee on House Administration of the U.S. House of Representatives, Azamichi Curiai. The interest of the Speaker and his colleagues in this case is apparent. It presents serious questions in our minds as to the continued viability of the speech or debate clause. At the outset, I would like to make one point clear. The Congress has read Johnson and Brewster, and the Congress accepts Johnson and Brewster. When we saw the solicitor's petition, however, and what we viewed as an attempt to relitigate Brewster, we were concerned. And that's why we are here. To paraphrase Thomas Jefferson's characterization of the clause, which he wrote shortly after the adoption of the Constitution, the clause is intended to protect the substance rather than the shadow of representative government. And for that reason, it states, for any speech or debate, they shall not be questioned in any other place. We believe that this clause operates as an institutional protection as well as a personalized privilege. And to affect this high principle of an unfettered legislative branch, the framers concluded that a jurisdictional allocation was necessary. And we read this jurisdictional allocation from the speech or debate clause read together with the punishment clause. Like other jurisdictional requirements, the trial of legislative acts must occur in the proper forum. It is not subject to waiver. Congressman Helstowski cannot waive himself into an Article III court for the trial of legislative acts. That is, even if he had voluntarily submitted all this material regarding his legislative act. That's our position. Even if he made an unequivocal, explicit waiver, knowing waiver, voluntarily. Yes. Any more than two... He was just... Any more than two litigants... Any more than two litigants could present themselves to an Article III court without a case of controversy and say we would like the court nevertheless to try this case. In other words, the speech or debate clause doesn't belong to an individual. It belongs to an institution. Is that your point? Yes. Well, if it does, why can't that institution provide for its waiver? Because the clause is a protection for the member as well, even as against a hostile Congress. So it's both. That's correct. Neither one can... It protects unpopular members as well as popular members, Democrats as well as Republicans. So Congress cannot, by however narrow a piece of legislation... That's right. ...provide for the executive prosecution of a legislative act... That's right. Any more than we could delegate impeachment, for instance. Mr. Brand, Congress, I assume, could amend the 201 and the other bribery statutes and say they do not apply to Congress. They could do that. Our position would be... Well, aren't you now doing that? No, sir. We don't believe we are. Well, aren't you trying to get us to do that? I don't think so. What we're saying is, as you said in Brewster, these cases can go forward without impugning legislative acts. And that's all we are saying here. The residual... You challenge the indictments, Mr. President? They're just the evidentiary... We do. You agree with Mr. Stavis? We do in this case. Although we agree also that there is nothing to prevent the U.S. attorney from taking the non-legislative material, presenting it to a new grand jury, and indicting and going forward to trial. Except maybe the statute of limitations. If that, in fact, is a problem. But you would, in that new indictment, or in those new grand jury proceedings, or in the subsequent trial, the evidence the government now proposes to use, you would say would be unusable? Correct. Hasn't Congress, or didn't Congress, take quite a long step in relation to the speech or debate clause when they've enacted these provisions? I don't think so, Your Honor. 201, like a plethora of other statutes regulating non-legislative behavior, has been passed by Congress in that context. We have statutes, for instance, 18 U.S.C. 431. It says that a member may not enter into a contract in which the United States is a party. That's not a legislative act. We regulate that by statute. We regulate campaign financing, because we say that when a member takes a political contribution, or campaigns for office, he is not engaging in the legislative process. And we regulate that through the United States Code. I don't believe you can read 201 in the context of the U.S. Code and the other ways in which we regulate members' conduct as the one example where we have attempted to put into Article III courts the trial of legislative acts. I don't believe that's consistent with the design of the Code at this time. At this point, we come to the question of the indictment. We would say that there having been neither a waiver nor a delegation under 201, the indictment at issue here, which charges legislative acts on the basis of what the grand jury heard, is fatally defective. And we say this for several reasons. This is not Calandra and the Fourth Amendment. This is not Costello and the Fifth Amendment. This is the speech of debate clause, which is part of the Constitution, which the framers placed in the Constitution, to protect questioning at the earliest possible juncture, not after indictment, when the death blow has been dealt as in this case. Well, to prevent question anywhere, in any other place. Correct. Why wouldn't your interest be served by, according to the congressman, a right to assert before the grand jury the privilege that you're talking about now? Our position would not deny him that. The grand jury which indicted him... Why wouldn't it be fully served? If he chooses not to assert it, then there is some form of waiver. Well, if it's never asserted, it never becomes an issue. But in this case, the grand jury which ultimately indicted him was one which there could be no waiver because he never appeared before that grand jury. What we're saying on the indictment issue is that the indictment is defective because the design of the speech of debate clause is to prevent questioning. If the questioning has already occurred and you are willing to say that that we will only, at trial, put on some evidentiary prescriptions, then you have not remedied the potential abuse which exists. But what was the questioning before the grand jury which violated the speech and debate clause? The legislative acts. But to whom were the questions addressed? I believe they were directed to the defendant. But why couldn't he then assert the speech and debate privilege and fully vindicate it by asserting it at that point and not having done so, he has waived it? Well, under Mr. Stavis' formulation, and I think we would agree with most of that, a member must answer as to third-party crime before a grand jury. But as soon as it reached him, is it not implied in both Johnson and the Brewster case that he not only need not answer, he may assert the proposition that he cannot be questioned? To give an example, if he were sued in a complaint in a civil case for a libel and the complaint alleged that the libel was committed on the floor of the House, could not the member of Congress simply informally tell the court by letter or any other way that he was not going to answer because the speech or debate clause protected him, and that he was not going to appear, and that any judgment entered on the basis of that complaint would be a nullity under the speech or debate clause. Well, as I... So that he... It is more than a quiet matter of not being questioned, or not answering, he can't even be questioned. Isn't that so? That's correct. Well, but he then submitted to the questioning here. Well, wouldn't he be... Wouldn't the same situation occur where he never appeared and the U.S. Attorney went to the Library of Congress and took the legislative material out of there? Is that a questioning? He would never have appeared to assert the privilege, yet we would assert that that's prohibited. Well, indeed you... That the grand jury can't hear. I thought you would assert that even if he appeared and answered freely, nevertheless... That's correct. As a claimant in an Article III court could come in and claim that he should get a remedy from the court. Well, Mr. Rand, you certainly don't need to... I know you say that the evidence should never have even been presented to the grand jury, but even if there was... Even if it was properly presented, or even if it could be said that he waived in some matter the presentation of the evidence, you still say that he never consented to be indicted, never consented to be threatened with indictment. And that would, of course, solve an awful lot of your problems if you went on that. Well, again, I believe that the heart of the clause is protection of the Congress from coordinate branches. And I gather, I thought your position was, so far does that principle go that nothing that he does before the grand jury can support an indictment. Correct. Nothing. Is that true? Mr. Brand, he didn't testify before this grand jury, did he? The one that he was indicted by? Yeah. No, he did not. He didn't testify before that grand jury. He did not. So your position has to be that evidence of legislative acts is inadmissible before the grand jury, even though the man himself is. But the clause doesn't read that way.
